newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major counters "time for a change" calls.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major counters "time for a change" calls.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major appealed to Britons on Friday not to throw him out of office just because it was "time for a change" after 17 years of Conservative rule.
Major, who trails badly in the opinion polls, said victory for the main opposition Labour party at the looming election could jeopardise the economic gains his government had overseen.

"Next year, Britain will go to the polls. People will have their democratic opportunity to decide if they wish to do away with the government that has enabled British people to build their success or choose instead the policies of those who have opposed all the ingredients of Britain's success," the prime minister told businessmen in Birmingham, central England.
"I know what some might say: "Isn't it time for a change?' Well, as long as you have progress, why bother to change?
"Britain's success is too valuable, too important to all of us to be put at risk," he added.

Major was speaking at the end of a week in which unemployment fell below two million for the first time in six years and the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development judged Britain's economic prospects to be the best in thirty years.
Unfortunately for Major, who must hold a general election by May, there is scant evidence yet of the economic good times translating into increased support for his Conservative party.
Polls consistently show Labour, which has been in opposition since 1979, with a lead of at least 20 percentage points.

Major blasted Labour for having opposed key privatisation changes, union reforms and public spending cuts and said it "could no more preserve the success of the British economy today than they could have helped to create it in the first place".
He said Britain's future in Europe would also be safer in Conservative hands, even though deep divisions in the ruling party over Europe have hamstrung the government in many areas.

Major, who earlier admitted in a television interview that Europe had become an "explosive emotional issue" in British politics", said he wanted to make Europe a success by using the same free-market policies that had made Britain a success.
Labour, by contrast, would meekly "follow in Europe's footsteps", Major said.

"So as we enter a momentous period for both Britain and Europe, people need to ask who they trust to be on their side to keep taxes down, prices stable and get more people back to work -- and who they trust to be on Britain's side in Europe in the crucial years ahead," Major said.
Labour's foreign affairs spokesman, Robin Cook, poured scorn on Major's speech. "The record shows that he never gets his way, that he constantly fails Britain and fails Britain's interests.
"John Major is a weak leader and the leader of a divided party. He cannot unite his party on Europe and he cannot effectively represent Britain's interests in Europe," Cook said.
Labour calls itself pro-European, but, like the Conservatives, it too has its "Euro-sceptics" who could make like difficult for leader Tony Blair if he captures power.
About 50 Labour Euro-sceptics warned Blair on Friday that an obsession with Europe could wreck the party's ambitious programme of constitutional reform and economic regeneration.

"If Labour fails, in its general election manifesto, to rule out joining the European single currency during the lifetime of the next parliament, the issue of the single currency will dominate that parliament and the life of the next Labour government," the group said in a statement.
